Anaphylaxis

criteria by organ system · epinephrine first · mimics · bradykinin swelling · hereditary angioedema attacksHow many systems are involved, and how soon after the exposure?

Source vignette Pt – 12 yo M, half an hour of burning, puffy eyes, a tight, scratchy throat and belly cramps, hours after starting amoxicillin for a sore throat; no known drug allergy · Exam – afebrile, blood pressure and pulse normal; swollen eyelids, mildly red conjunctivae, wheals on the trunk · Q – the mechanism; options included Epstein-Barr virus infection, immune complexes, impaired bradykinin breakdown, mast cell activation and vasculitis

1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Skin or mucosa plus one more system (airway, persistent gut symptoms or circulation) within minutes to hours of a likely allergen is anaphylaxis, and hypotension is not required; low blood pressure alone after a known allergen also qualifies.
  • Give intramuscular (IM) epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh first; antihistamines, albuterol and glucocorticoids are adjuncts that never replace it.
  • Swelling with no hives on an ACE inhibitor (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor), or with a low complement C4 level, is bradykinin angioedema; a rash days into a drug is a delayed reaction, not anaphylaxis.
What it is

An acute, potentially fatal systemic allergic reaction: immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated, type I hypersensitivity in a sensitized person re-exposed to the antigen.

Driver

Mast cell and basophil degranulation. IgE type: the antigen cross-links IgE on sensitized cells.

Non-IgE type (anaphylactoid): direct mast cell activation, no prior sensitization, clinically identical.

Triggers

Foods (nuts, eggs, seafood); drugs (beta-lactams, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs); insect venom; latex; radiocontrast (non-IgE)

Selective immunoglobulin A (IgA) deficiency: may react to blood products non-modifiable

Chain

Sensitized mast cells and basophils meet the antigen

histamine, tryptase and leukotrienes are released

vasodilation and plasma leakage; smooth muscle contraction

hives, airway swelling, wheeze, vomiting; distributive shock with warm skin

Insights

Shock can be the only sign: cardiovascular collapse can occur without respiratory or other symptoms, which is why low blood pressure alone after a known allergen is a criterion.

A first reaction is not a first exposure: an earlier, uneventful course sensitized the mast cells.

Minutesonset; shock can develop this fast
Within 2 hoursbest window for a serum tryptase
4 to 6 hourstypical biphasic window, with no re-exposure
2Urgent risks
Act now
FindingAction
Stridor or wheeze that does not answer epinephrineOxygen and early intubation; waiting may let airway edema progress.
Hypotension that persists after IM epinephrineIsotonic intravenous (IV) fluids, which usually work; IV epinephrine, preferably as an infusion, may be given next.
Reaction in a patient taking a beta-blockerGive epinephrine anyway; if hypotension persists, add IV glucagon (step 7, rung 4).
3Differential
Anaphylaxis and its mimics
DiagnosisDecides itNext best step
Acute urticaria aloneHives and itch, but no second system: airway, gut and blood pressure are normal; mast cell activation, often IgE.Treat the hives with an oral antihistamine; epinephrine is not needed.
Bradykinin angioedema (ACE inhibitor, hereditary angioedema)Over hours: swelling of the lips, tongue or bowel wall without hives or itch; on an ACE inhibitor it can begin after months or years of use. C1 inhibitor normally blocks kallikrein, which makes bradykinin; ACE breaks bradykinin down, so an ACE inhibitor lets it build. Hereditary angioedema is autosomal dominant C1 inhibitor deficiency that presents in childhood or adolescence, with colicky abdominal attacks from swelling of the bowel wall.Stop the ACE inhibitor; check C4 when no drug explains it.
Vasovagal syncopeSeconds after pain or fear, such as a needle; a vagal surge gives bradycardia, pallor and sweat, with no hives or wheeze.Check the pulse: slow, with clear skin and lungs, is vagal, not anaphylaxis.
Serum sickness-like reaction 5 to 14 days into a drug: urticarial rash with fever, joint pain and nodes; a delayed drug hypersensitivity (true serum sickness is immune complex).Stop the drug; it resolves on its own.
Epstein-Barr virus rash with an aminopenicillin (infectious mononucleosis)Days into amoxicillin: a maculopapular rash, fever, exudative tonsils, posterior neck nodes and left upper quadrant pain.Treat as a virus-driven rash, not an IgE penicillin allergy.
IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura)Days; immune complex vessel inflammation: palpable purpura, fever, joint pain, colicky abdominal pain.Examine the rash: palpable purpura is not urticaria.
Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (postinfectious glomerulonephritis) Weeks, not days: about 1 to 3 weeks after strep throat, up to about 6 weeks after impetigo. Swelling that builds over days, with high blood pressure and cola-colored urine.Check the blood pressure and urine: immune complex nephritis, not anaphylaxis.
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
No known drug allergy; first reactionSensitized by an earlier, uneventful exposureTreat as anaphylaxis.
Hypotension alone after a known allergenAnaphylaxis by the third criterionGive IM epinephrine now.
Swelling unchanged after epinephrine and an antihistamineBradykinin, not mast cellStop any ACE inhibitor; in hereditary angioedema give C1 inhibitor concentrate (step 7); secure the airway if it closes. More epinephrine is usually not effective.
Flushing and hives after fishScombroid fish poisoning can mimic it: flushing, hives, diarrhea and cramps minutes to hours after eatingGive an antihistamine; albuterol or epinephrine may be added if needed.
Pause point
Hives, throat tightness and cramps; blood pressure normal Offered as wait for hypotension or an oral antihistamine How many systems, and how soon after the exposure? → Anaphylaxis: three systems within minutes; give IM epinephrine
Lip and tongue swelling, no hives, on lisinopril Offered as repeat epinephrine or mast cell activation Are there hives or itch? → Bradykinin angioedema: stop the ACE inhibitor
Urticarial rash, fever and joint pain a week into penicillin Offered as anaphylaxis or acute rheumatic fever Minutes, or days? → Serum sickness-like reaction: stop the drug

Epinephrine comes first; antihistamines and glucocorticoids never replace it.

5Diagnostic criteria
Anaphylaxis is likely with any 1
CriterionRequires
First: skin or mucosaHives, flushing or swelling of the lips, tongue or eyes, with breathing trouble or low blood pressure
Second: likely allergen2 or more of skin or mucosa, respiratory, low blood pressure, persistent gastrointestinal symptoms
Third: known allergenLow blood pressure alone
Low blood pressure in a childAge-specific low systolic pressure or a fall of more than 30%
6Severity
Severity findings
FindingMeaning
Respiratory distress or hypotensionSevere: admit for prolonged observation
2 or more IM doses, or any IV epinephrine, neededAdmit for prolonged observation; higher biphasic risk
Rash alone, or resolved with 1 doseMay be discharged sooner
Taking a beta-blockerRisk factor for a severe reaction
7Treatment
1

FirstCriteria met

IM epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh: 0.01 mL/kg of the 1 mg/mL (1:1000) solution in children, 0.3 to 0.5 mL in adults. Absorption is greatest from the anterolateral thigh muscle.

2

PersistingSymptoms persist after 5 to 15 minutes

Repeat IM epinephrine.

3

AirwayStridor or wheeze despite epinephrine

Oxygen and early intubation.

4

ShockHypotension persists

Isotonic IV fluids, which usually work; IV epinephrine, preferably as an infusion, may be given next; IV glucagon for a patient on a beta-blocker.

5

AdjunctsAfter epinephrine

Antihistamines (diphenhydramine), inhaled albuterol for persistent bronchospasm; glucocorticoids are unproven, though they may help head off a late-phase reaction.

Hereditary angioedema: attacks and prevention
SituationDo
Laryngeal swelling with stridor or the airway closingSecure the airway first; airway swelling is usually the cause of death
Laryngeal swelling with the airway still openGive C1 inhibitor concentrate now and be ready to secure the airway; intubation may be needed in severe cases
Acute attackC1 inhibitor concentrate, icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor blocker) or ecallantide (kallikrein inhibitor); epinephrine, antihistamines and glucocorticoids are usually not effective
Needs a blood pressure drugAvoid ACE inhibitors
Triggers to plan aroundDental work and other minor trauma; estrogen-containing medications
First-degree relativesScreen with C1 inhibitor and C4 levels, with or without symptoms
8Follow-up
After the reaction
SituationDo
Symptoms resolvedObserve for several hours: a biphasic reaction typically returns within 4 to 6 hours
DischargeEpinephrine autoinjector for every patient (0.15 mg child, 0.3 mg adult), alert identification, avoid the trigger
Anaphylaxis to an insect stingDesensitization, since stings cannot reliably be avoided
Anaphylaxis after a vaccine dose No further doses of that vaccine
Practice
  1. 12 yo M, 30 minutes after starting amoxicillin for strep throat; a course at age 5 caused no reaction. Itchy wheals on the trunk, puffy eyelids, a tight throat and crampy abdominal pain; BP 116/68, HR 92 → Mast cell activation → anaphylaxis: skin, respiratory and gastrointestinal involvement within 30 minutes of amoxicillin, after sensitization by an earlier course; intramuscular (IM) epinephrine
  2. 7 yo F at a birthday party, 10 minutes after eating a cookie made with peanut butter, develops hives on the face and trunk, wheezing and 2 episodes of vomiting; no previous reactions to food; T 37.0, BP 98/60, HR 128, RR 30, SpO2 94% on room air; diffuse expiratory wheezes → Intramuscular epinephrine → anaphylaxis by skin plus respiratory and gastrointestinal involvement; blood pressure need not fall
  3. 9 yo M, itchy raised wheals on the trunk and arms 1 hour after eating strawberries for the first time this season; no lip or tongue swelling, throat symptoms, cough, vomiting or abdominal pain; BP 104/66, HR 90, SpO2 99%; lungs clear; blanching urticarial plaques → Oral cetirizine → acute urticaria alone: one system, so criteria for anaphylaxis are not met
  4. 15 yo M treated in the emergency department for hives, throat tightness and wheezing 20 minutes after eating cashews, his first reaction to food; one dose of intramuscular epinephrine was given, and after 6 hours of observation he is asymptomatic with normal vital signs and clear lungs → Epinephrine autoinjector prescription → anaphylaxis, observed for a biphasic reaction; discharge with self-injectable epinephrine, an action plan, avoidance and allergy referral
  5. 58 yo M with hypertension and diabetes, 6 hours of progressive swelling of the lips and tongue; no itching, hives, wheezing or abdominal pain; takes lisinopril, which he started 2 years ago, and metformin; no new foods or medications; swelling did not improve after intramuscular epinephrine and diphenhydramine → Impaired bradykinin degradation → ACE inhibitor angioedema: no urticaria and little response to epinephrine; stop the ACE inhibitor permanently
  6. 16 yo F with recurrent episodes over 3 years of painless, nonpruritic swelling of the hands, face and once the throat, each lasting 2 to 3 days, and separate episodes of colicky abdominal pain with vomiting; no hives; takes no medications; her mother has similar episodes; antihistamines and epinephrine have not helped; examination between episodes is normal → Serum C4 level → hereditary angioedema from C1 inhibitor deficiency; low C4, bradykinin-mediated, so epinephrine disappoints
  7. 17 yo F, 5 days of fever, sore throat and fatigue, treated with amoxicillin for presumed strep pharyngitis; 4 days later, a diffuse, mildly itchy maculopapular rash on the trunk and limbs; T 38.4, BP 112/70; tonsillar exudates, tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, left upper quadrant tenderness; no wheals, no lip swelling, lungs clear → Infectious mononucleosis → an aminopenicillin rash during Epstein-Barr virus infection; not an IgE-mediated penicillin allergy
  8. 34 yo F with a known severe shellfish allergy becomes lightheaded 15 minutes after eating a dish she later learns contained shrimp; no rash, flushing, lip swelling, wheeze or vomiting; BP 76/44, HR 132, warm extremities; lungs clear → Anaphylaxis → hypotension alone after a known allergen meets criteria; give IM epinephrine
  9. 22 yo F with recurrent episodes since adolescence of painless, nonpruritic swelling of the lips and one hand lasting 2 to 3 days, the latest starting the day after a dental extraction; separate bouts of colicky abdominal pain with vomiting; no hives; takes a combined oral contraceptive and no other medications; her father has similar episodes; epinephrine and diphenhydramine in the emergency department did not help; serum C4 low → C1 inhibitor deficiency → hereditary angioedema: bradykinin-mediated swelling without urticaria; confirm with C1 inhibitor level and function
  10. 19 yo M with known hereditary angioedema, 4 hours of progressive swelling of the face and tongue with a hoarse voice after a facial injury in a basketball game; no stridor; SpO2 98% on room air; no hives; no improvement after intramuscular epinephrine and intravenous diphenhydramine → Intravenous C1 inhibitor concentrate → acute hereditary angioedema attack with laryngeal involvement: give specific therapy and be ready to secure the airway
  11. 45 yo F with hereditary angioedema, low C4 and a family history, now with blood pressure 152/96 on three separate visits; no diabetes or kidney disease → Lisinopril → ACE inhibitors block bradykinin breakdown and provoke attacks
Pearls Waiting for hypotension delays epinephrine: throat tightness or wheeze with hives already meets the criteria · The diagnosis is clinical; a serum tryptase within 2 hours can support it afterward but never delays treatment · Swelling with no hives is bradykinin, where epinephrine works poorly: stop the ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor, and check C4 when swelling recurs without a drug · Common triggers are foods (nuts, eggs, seafood), drugs such as beta-lactams, and insect venom
Pairs with Fever and Rash in a Child covers the serum sickness-like reaction: did the hives start 5 to 14 days into the drug, with joint pain? Transfusion Reactions covers anaphylaxis during transfusion: is the recipient IgA deficient? Shock in Children covers anaphylactic shock as a distributive subtype: is perfusion abnormal? Stool Changes in a Well Infant covers FPIES (food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome), the non-IgE mimic: is it hours of vomiting without hives? Childhood Vaccine Schedule and Contraindications covers anaphylaxis after a vaccine dose as a contraindication: did it follow an earlier dose of the same vaccine? Child with Puffy Eyes places the acute allergic reaction among the other causes of swollen eyelids: is it one eye or both, and does the urine contain protein?
Transferable rule Skin or mucosal involvement plus any second system within minutes to hours of an exposure is anaphylaxis. Treat it with IM (intramuscular) epinephrine first. Swelling with no hives points to bradykinin. A rash that arrives days later points to a delayed drug or immune complex reaction.
Unchecked attributeImpaired bradykinin degradation: the swollen eyes suggest angioedema, but bradykinin swelling has no wheals or itch; he has wheals on the trunk plus throat and gut symptoms, which is mast cell release.
Unchecked attributeImmune complex formation: the sore throat invites poststreptococcal disease or serum sickness, but immune complexes take days to form; this began within hours of the drug, not days.
True-fact-wrong-slotEpstein-Barr virus infection: mononucleosis really does cause a rash after amoxicillin, but that rash is maculopapular, comes days later and brings fever and nodes; he is afebrile with wheals.
Salient decoySystemic vasculitis: crampy abdominal pain recalls IgA vasculitis, but vasculitis develops over days with fever and palpable purpura, not wheals within minutes.
